paper.title: Accelerating Constrained Decoding with Token Space Compression

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-7 and Limitations; proofs in Appendices B-C and the stack-adjacency algorithm in D skimmed

claims.claim: The cost of grammar-constrained decoding with complex context-free grammars can be cut to near that of unconstrained generation, without changing a single output, by grouping vocabulary tokens into classes that are provably interchangeable with respect to the grammar, so that the grammar engine checks only one representative per class at each step. Supported only if the constrained outputs are byte-identical with and without the compression (guaranteed by construction); if the offline grouping takes at most a few seconds per tokenizer-grammar pair and shrinks the vocabulary by at least 40 to 1; if on complex grammars (C++ and a brace-delimited Python variant) it reduces the state-of-the-art engine's unbatched overhead by an order of magnitude; and if at batch sizes of 8 and 16 on the hardest grammar total generation time stays within about three times that of unconstrained generation, where the engine alone is around a hundred times slower or does not finish within 24 hours.
claims.decision_rule: Lossless (identical outputs); precompute <=~2 s and >=40:1 compression; ~9-45x lower unbatched overhead on C++/Bython; batched Bython <=~3x unconstrained where XGrammar2 >=~100x or times out.

claims.claim: Forcing a language model's output to follow a context-free grammar pays off mainly for small models and for unfamiliar formal languages, not for common formats a capable model already writes well. Supported only if, for a programming language the models rarely see (Python rewritten with braces and semicolons), constrained decoding at least quadruples functional correctness for every model tested, from a 3B to a 20B model; while for JSON, XML and C++ the two larger models' functional correctness changes by under 3 points with constraints; and if the smallest model improves on every format.
claims.decision_rule: Bython functional correctness >= 4x for all 3 models; JSON/XML/C++ functional change < 3 pts for Qwen-4B and GPT-20B; Llama-3B improves on all four tasks.

experiments.text: Fix tasks, grammars, models and measurements. Setup: four structured-generation tasks with syntactic and functional correctness: 100 JSON-schema queries (json-mode-eval; executes, keys and values match the reference), 200 XML instances from StructEval (parses; dot-path rules satisfied), the 164 C++ problems of HumanEval-X (compiles; passes tests), and the same 164 problems translated into Bython, Python with braces and semicolons, with a description of Bython in the system prompt (compiles to Python; passes tests). Grammars: XGrammar2's JSON-schema builder, an XML 1.1 EBNF adapted to GBNF, a published C++ grammar and a Bython grammar written from scratch. Models Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct and gpt-oss-20b, temperature 0.2, at most 500 tokens, five seeds, one H100 with grammar work on a 16-thread Xeon; batch sizes 1, 8 and 16 except JSON (one grammar per request, batch 1).

Group tokens by how they act on the grammar. Setup: convert the grammar to Greibach normal form (only to compute classes; the engine keeps the original grammar) and, for each vocabulary token, compute its displacement: the set of (input stack, output stack) pairs it can produce in the resulting pushdown automaton, pruning backtracking with a precomputed stack-adjacency relation. Tokens with identical displacements are provably interchangeable (a refinement of syntactic congruence), so masks computed on class representatives (the shortest token in each class) can be mapped back to the full vocabulary with a gather. The engine (XGrammar2, the only one found able to handle these grammars) is initialised with the representatives only.

Measure pre-computation cost and compression. Setup: wall-clock time and number of classes per tokenizer and grammar. Result: 0.28-1.80 seconds per pair; vocabularies of 128,256-201,088 tokens shrink to about 253-258 classes for JSON (mean over the 100 schemas), 1,517-1,591 for XML, 2,815-3,095 for C++ and 1,783-2,011 for Bython, compression from about 40:1 (Llama, C++) to about 800:1 (gpt-oss, JSON).

Measure end-to-end generation time with and without compression. Setup: mean seconds per instance, including the language model, for unconstrained decoding, XGrammar2 and XGrammar2 with compression, at batch sizes 1, 8 and 16. Result: unbatched, the engine alone costs about 2x on C++ and 7-9x on Bython (Llama 12.55 s vs 1.39 s unconstrained) and compression brings Bython to 1.76 s; at batch 8 on Bython the engine alone takes 44.51 s (Llama) and 97.07 s (Qwen) and times out for gpt-oss, against 0.59, 1.40 and 1.89 s with compression (unconstrained 0.25, 0.45, 1.50), about 75x faster; at batch 16 the engine alone times out on Bython for all three models while compression stays at 0.50-2.11 s. On C++ at batch 16 the engine alone takes 0.85-10.49 s against 0.35-1.56 s compressed. Per-token engine overhead falls 9-45x.

Check where compression does not help. Setup: the same timings on the simple JSON-schema grammars, one per request. Result: JSON overhead is already small (Llama 3.60 s vs 3.42 s unconstrained) and compression barely changes it (3.52 s), and because each schema needs its own grouping, the 0.28-0.49 s pre-computation can exceed the time saved for one-off lightweight grammars.

Compare correctness with and without grammar constraints. Result (syntactic / functional %): on Bython, constrained decoding raises Llama from 6.7 / 2.3 to 52.1 / 9.2, Qwen from 2.2 / 1.0 to 43.3 / 18.9 and gpt-oss from 13.0 / 10.8 to 72.0 / 46.9. For the larger models on familiar formats the change is small: Qwen JSON 76.5 to 74.7 functional, XML 61.1 to 61.4, C++ 70.6 to 72.7; gpt-oss JSON 80.2 to 81.2, XML 60.1 to 59.0, C++ 41.2 to 40.2. The 3B model gains everywhere (JSON functional 13.9 to 73.7, XML 7.1 to 16.3, C++ 30.5 to 32.7). Syntactic correctness is mostly below 100% even with constraints because outputs cut off at 500 tokens are valid prefixes but not complete programs.

dropped: Proofs of losslessness and of the refinement property (theory); qualitative example of class colouring.
notes: CFGzip outputs are byte-identical to XGrammar2's, so correctness is reported once for the constrained engine.
